blocks.text: ...and meeting each other without stress

Socialisation techniques are practical, purposeful exercises and actions in everyday life that serve to make encounters with other dogs and with other participants in a situation as pleasant and free of complications as possible.
They are based on the experience that, when in doubt, our dog retreats to “safe” territory or gathers experience by observing from a distance.
From this, various techniques can be derived that allow us both to shape encounter situations actively and to influence them in a de-escalating way.
Definition and advantage 🐕

Sending the dog out with the cue “Go” is suitable for encounter situations in which we want to give our dog the option of stepping aside and taking up an observing resting position while the other party passes us and our dog.

The “Go” procedure shows a comparatively quick and positive training progression. With constant use, a kind of automation sets in – our dog will soon carry out this procedure willingly and without much instruction.
Prerequisites and training basics 📋
Prerequisite: Our dog should respond to its name and have at least a basic command of the cues “Sit” and “Down”.

Training environment: The first training sessions take place without distraction. As training progresses, we apply the exercise with increasing distraction – but always only in such a way that, given the situation, it is foreseeable that the exercise can be completed successfully.
Leash: In the beginning we train on the leash. A minimum leash length of 2 metres is recommended.
Step 1: Addressing the dog 🗣️
While walking, we address our dog by name in a calm and friendly voice. It is important that we do not trigger any state of alarm.
Step 2: Initiating the sending out 👉
At the moment our dog responds to its name, we turn towards the edge of the path, point towards the edge of the path with our free hand and calmly say “Go” to the dog.
We walk relaxed together with the dog beyond the edge of the path and, with light help from the leash, try to let the dog walk slightly ahead. Our own action serves as a model.
The goal is for the dog to recognise that the cue “Go” is the signal to take up a position away from the path, or at least at the edge of the path.
Step 3: Positioning and securing 📍
Once we have sent our dog to the desired position, we say “Sit” or “Down” in a calm but firm tone of voice. The dog should turn towards us while doing so.
We should preferably orient our dog towards the reliable “Down”. As long as “Down” is not yet sufficiently established, we can also use “Sit”.

Note that the dog is brought into “Sit” or “Down” at the desired position with active help and should not first come back towards us. The help is provided by calm guidance with the lead. The dog should then stay calmly in position and, if necessary, be corrected back into it quickly if it gets up incorrectly.
Step 4: Waiting and ending the exercise ⏱️

We calmly move away from the dog to the length of the leash and leave it in its place for a certain time. In the early stages we end the procedure by stepping up to the dog and conclude the exercise with “Sit” and intensive praise – optionally supplemented with play and a treat.

A calm sit in front of us ends the exercise. We take our time over the whole procedure and thereby show the dog that encounters are not a problem, at least from our side, and that moving aside to a safe position is a good alternative for feeling comfortable.
Step 5: Progress and variations 📈

Once the procedure is established through regular daily training and the dog stays reliably in its place even when people and dogs walk past, we can move on to calling the dog to us after the encounter instead of fetching it.

This universally applicable exercise can be varied as needed: We can send our dog off the path and bring it into “Sit” or “Down” while we ourselves remain standing on the path. Alternatively, in difficult situations, we can move together with our dog to a position off to the side, and there place and secure the dog in “Sit” or “Down”, facing away from the encounter situation.
The affectionate, calm praise at the end, supplemented with play and a treat as needed, puts our dog in a positive state of expectation, which places the next exercise on a successful foundation.
Distance and increasing the difficulty 📏

For all variants: Learning success depends on encounters running with little stress. We therefore make a deliberate choice between “Sit” and “Down”, depending on the expected difficulty of the situation.

At the beginning we choose a generous distance from the other party. A good guideline is at least 6 metres. As training confidence grows, this distance is reduced step by step until finally placing our dog at the edge of the path is sufficient.
Important notes ⚠️
Avoid harsh or loud cues during training and in everyday use.
Avoid keeping the leash short.
Avoid carrying out exercises in the direction of the distraction.
Avoid praising too early while the situation is still ongoing.
Avoid stress throughout the entire procedure.
Avoid the dog leaving the exercise position on its own.
Avoid ending the exercise too early, which would result in the dog breaking out of the situation uncontrolled.
Practical impulse: Shaping conscious encounters

On your walk, actively look for situations with little distraction in which to practise “Go”. Begin with a distance of at least 6 metres from the other party and reduce it step by step. With every encounter handled calmly, your dog’s trust grows – and so does its willingness to go to its safe position voluntarily.
→ Did I make sure at the start that the environment was calm and free of distraction?
→ Did I train daily and repeatedly?
→ Did I address the dog calmly by name and wait for its response?
→ Did I purposefully walk with the dog to the edge of the path using the calm cue “Go”?
→ Was the support with the leash stress-free and fluid?
→ Did I place the dog clearly recognisably away from the path?
→ Did I carry out “Sit” or “Down” calmly and promptly?
→ Did I leave the dog in its position for long enough?
→ Did I end the exercise calmly and praise generously?
→ Did I pay attention to pauses between the individual steps?
→ When applying it under real distraction, did I send the dog out far enough, or did I walk out of the situation together with it far enough?
→ Did I let the situation fade away for long enough before I ended and released the exercise?
→ Did I praise calmly and intensively?
